items.title: Exposure matters more than persuasiveness for digital mass persuasion
items.author: Ben M. Tappin
items.content: The persuasive impact of digital media content depends both on its persuasiveness per person and on how many people are exposed to it, and there is greater variability in exposure than persuasiveness across content. Together, these facts suggest exposure matters more than persuasiveness for digital mass persuasion.

items.title: Fifty-five crowdsourced designs assessing carbon pricing support in the USA
items.author: Xian Zhao
items.content: In 55 experiments involving nearly 20,000 US residents, behavioural efforts to build public support for carbon pricing raised support by only 1.1–2.4 percentage points.

items.title: Multidimensional motor unit control after paralysing spinal cord injury using non-invasive recordings
items.author: Juan Alvaro Gallego
items.content: Yang, Rawji, Gibbs and colleagues show that participants with spinal cord injury can modulate the activity of motor units from their paralysed hand to control a computer cursor in 3D, play video games and drive a virtual wheelchair.

items.title: Research that will survive a fast-paced world
items.author: Gerd Gigerenzer
items.content: Crises and technological waves pull science towards fast, trend-driven work. But a drift towards timely research might negatively affect quality and limit the methods, infrastructure and datasets that accumulate value slowly. We discuss how researchers, funders and journals can draw lasting value from urgency-driven research.

items.title: Neural interface without a scalpel
items.author: Michael Dimitriou
items.content: For people who are paralysed by spinal cord injury, regaining hand use is a top priority. Yet the most capable neural interfaces have relied on surgically implanted electrodes. Yang, Rawji, Gibbs and colleagues show that individual motor units, read non-invasively using surface electrodes, can deliver multidimensional control even amid involuntary background muscle activity.

items.title: Behavioural interventions shift carbon-pricing support only slightly
items.content: Across 55 independently designed experiments with 19,558 participants from the USA, behavioural interventions produced a small increase in support for carbon pricing. Participating researchers substantially overestimated these effects.
